name: Torticollis stretching

lead: Torticollis, or wry neck, is an abnormal tilt or rotation of the head, most often involving the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle. In infants, congenital muscular torticollis is treated first with gentle stretching, positioning and physical therapy.

In looksmaxxing talk, stretching a tight SCM is raised as a way to improve head posture and neck or face asymmetry. The evidence summarized here is for infants; Wikipedia reports that about 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care.

paras: Stretching and positioning aim to lengthen the shortened SCM and restore neck range of motion. In infants this is paired with caregiver education such as alternating feeding sides and supervised tummy time.

Adult or later-onset torticollis can have neurological or structural causes, including cervical dystonia and atlanto-axial rotatory fixation, which are medically managed, for example with botulinum toxin. Sources recommend evaluation to exclude underlying causes.

lead: Torticollis, commonly called wry neck, is a condition in which neck muscles, most often the sternocleidomastoid, produce an abnormal tilt, turn or flexion of the head. It may be congenital, acquired, or spasmodic (cervical dystonia).[1][2]

Stretching, positioning and physical therapy are the usual first-line approach for congenital muscular torticollis in infants. Wikipedia reports that 85 to 90 percent of congenital cases resolve with conservative care and that stretching fails in about 5 to 10 percent, who then may need surgery.[2]

Orthopedic literature also notes that long-standing torticollis in young patients can come with flattening on one side of the face.[3] No studies found examined stretching for facial appearance in otherwise healthy adults.

paras: Torticollis is classified by head position as laterocollis (tilt), rotational torticollis, anterocollis or retrocollis, and by timing as congenital, acquired or spasmodic.[2] Congenital muscular torticollis is the most common type and is usually linked to a shortened SCM, sometimes with a firm mass appearing in the first weeks of life.[2] Grokipedia reports an incidence of roughly 1 in 250 infants.[1]

Physical therapy components include passive and active range-of-motion work, symmetrical movement, environmental changes and caregiver education, such as alternating feeding sides and supervised prone positioning.[2] Grokipedia says the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends early physical therapy and positioning for congenital cases and advises against head-shaping pillows.[1]

Wikipedia reports that over 98% of infants treated before 1 month recover by 2.5 months, that home therapy by parents was reported as effective as outpatient therapy, and that manipulation alone showed little benefit over placebo but added benefit when combined with physical therapy.[2]

For adult cervical dystonia, a 1986 double-blind trial in 21 patients found botulinum toxin A produced subjective and objective improvement, including pain relief in 14 of 16 patients with pain, with side effects more often reported on placebo.[4] A randomised, sham-controlled trial examined pallidal neurostimulation in medication-refractory cervical dystonia,[5] and a 1994 report examined the development of resistance to botulinum toxin in torticollis patients.[6]
No studies found on stretching for facial symmetry or aesthetics.

A 1977 series described irreversible atlanto-axial rotatory fixation, in which all 17 patients had torticollis and restricted, often painful neck motion, with delayed diagnosis common and facial flattening in seven young patients with long-standing deformity.[3] Other causes include ocular problems, tumors and neurological disorders, and diagnosis relies on history and examination with imaging where indicated.[1]
Stretching a tight SCM is discussed in appearance-focused circles as a way to improve head posture and neck or face asymmetry. The published evidence concerns infants and neurological torticollis.
